topicName: Balanced Trees: AVL Trees, Red-Black Trees
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Balanced Trees: AVL Trees and Red-Black Trees"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"In the realm of data structures and algorithms, balanced trees play a crucial role in maintaining efficient search, insertion, and deletion operations. Unlike their unbalanced counterparts, balanced trees guarantee a logarithmic time complexity for these operations in the worst-case scenario. This tutorial explores two prominent types of balanced trees: AVL trees and Red-Black trees."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"AVL Trees"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"AVL trees, named after their inventors Adelson-Velsky and Landis, are self-balancing binary search trees. The key characteristic of an AVL tree is that for every node, the height difference between its left and right subtrees (called the balance factor) is at most 1. This constraint ensures that the tree remains relatively balanced, preventing it from degenerating into a linked list-like structure."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Balance Factor and Rotations"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"The balance factor of a node is calculated as the height of its left subtree minus the height of its right subtree. An AVL tree maintains its balance by performing rotations when the balance factor of a node becomes less than -1 or greater than 1. There are four types of rotations:"},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Right Rotation: Used when the balance factor is greater than 1 and the left subtree is left-heavy."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Left Rotation: Used when the balance factor is less than -1 and the right subtree is right-heavy."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Left-Right Rotation: Used when the balance factor is greater than 1 and the left subtree is right-heavy."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Right-Left Rotation: Used when the balance factor is less than -1 and the right subtree is left-heavy."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"AVL Tree Operations"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Insertion: When inserting a new node, we perform a standard binary search tree insertion. After insertion, we traverse up the tree from the inserted node, updating the balance factors of the ancestors. If a balance factor becomes invalid, we perform the necessary rotations to restore balance."},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Deletion: Deletion in an AVL tree is similar to insertion. After deleting a node, we traverse up the tree, updating balance factors and performing rotations as needed."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Red-Black Trees"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Red-Black trees are another type of self-balancing binary search tree. They use a different approach to maintain balance compared to AVL trees. Each node in a Red-Black tree is colored either red or black. These colors are used to enforce certain properties that guarantee logarithmic height."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Red-Black Tree Properties"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"A Red-Black tree must satisfy the following properties:"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Every node is either red or black."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The root is always black."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Every leaf (NIL node) is black."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"If a node is red, then both its children are black."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"For each node, all simple paths from the node to descendant leaves contain the same number of black nodes (the 'black-height')."},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Red-Black Tree Operations"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"Insertion: Insertion in a Red-Black tree involves a standard binary search tree insertion followed by recoloring and rotations to maintain the Red-Black tree properties. Cases involving different color combinations of the node, its parent, and its uncle are handled to ensure balance."},{"order":25,"type":"paragraph","text":"Deletion: Deletion is more complex than insertion. It also involves recoloring and rotations to restore the Red-Black tree properties after a node is removed."},{"order":26,"type":"subheading","text":"Comparison of AVL and Red-Black Trees"},{"order":27,"type":"paragraph","text":"AVL trees are more rigidly balanced than Red-Black trees. This means that AVL trees provide faster lookups because the height is strictly minimized. However, the frequent rotations required to maintain this strict balance can make insertion and deletion operations slower compared to Red-Black trees."},{"order":28,"type":"paragraph","text":"Red-Black trees offer a better balance between search speed and insertion/deletion speed. They require fewer rotations than AVL trees, making them suitable for applications where insertions and deletions are frequent."},{"order":29,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":30,"type":"paragraph","text":"Both AVL trees and Red-Black trees are valuable data structures for maintaining balanced search trees. The choice between them depends on the specific application requirements. If lookups are the primary operation, AVL trees might be preferred. If insertions and deletions are frequent, Red-Black trees might be a better choice."}]
